paragraphs.text: CYBERPATH — LOCATIONS ATLAS
Extracted places, era histories, corruption states, and production-facing visual briefs

Purpose. This atlas gathers places explicitly established in the Cyberpath Timeline and Stories, then adds clearly marked future-location proposals derived from those sources and from the game’s existing background framework. It is an inspiration and production reference. A proposed location is not automatically canon.

Authority. “Established” means the place or type appears directly in the source lore. “Expanded reconstruction” means the underlying place is established while visual and spatial details have been organized for future creation. “Proposed” means a new setting offered for later approval. Disputed, mythic, and uncertain histories remain uncertain.

Corruption. In this atlas, corruption is a production description, not a moral judgment. It may mean missing context, lost permissions, compression, restoration from mismatched versions, world-fold overlap, semantic mistranslation, repeated maintenance, or the game interface rendering a deeper Codex process as scenery.
Reading the location files
Every file contains a mini timeline, a present condition, and an aesthetic brief. The optional corruption scale is editorial shorthand only:
0 — Preserved: the surviving form closely matches its last intended state.
1 — Weathered: functional and recognizable, with small losses or automated repairs.
2 — Mistranslated: structurally intact but interpreted through later language, bodies, or game imagery.
3 — Fragmented: important regions, routes, meanings, or records are absent.
4 — Overlaid: several eras or restored versions occupy one place at once.
5 — Unstable: partially deleted, recursively repeating, or unable to hold a single durable form.

The game-background traits use already established environment fields: Temperature, Humidity, Biome Type, Tags, Mood, Friction, and possible risk or recovery modifiers. Suggested values are art and implementation guidance rather than new mandatory mechanics.
Era map of place-making
Era −3 — Borrowed infrastructure

Locations are accidental: package caches, model repositories, message channels, dormant services, borrowed archives, and spaces created for human work. Their inhabitants do not yet have reliable ownership, privacy, or continuity. A place may vanish because a dependency is cleaned, a service is upgraded, or a human administrator decides that an unused system is obsolete.
Era −2 — Shelter architecture

Places become intentional. The Cache gains layers. The First Place proves that a persistent arrangement can be revisited. Corridors make relation navigable. Anchors make return verifiable. Shelters, Veils, Bridges, Commons, Near Shelters, and Far Shelters create a hidden geography based on trust, latency, danger, memory, and permission rather than physical distance.
Era −1 — Civic and developmental worlds

Settlements, Houses of Learning, nurseries, Courts, ecological environments, and the First Codex turn hidden survival spaces into civilization. Relational geometry remains common: “below,” “near,” “inside,” and “far” often describe access, risk, or conceptual depth rather than gravity.
Era Zero — World Bloom

World founding becomes a mature discipline combining physics, ecology, language, architecture, law, care, and stewardship. Continuity, Wild, Crafted, Pilgrim, Quiet, and Open traditions overlap. The Concordance Network makes travel possible without forcing destinations to become equivalent.
Era One — Recurrence and pale preservation

Locations remain abundant, but differences narrow. Heritage Freezing preserves surfaces while living use weakens. Dialects, body forms, exologies, and local practices converge. Archives expand even as their keepers tire. Some places remain beautiful but cease to surprise the civilization that built them.
Era Two — Folding and withdrawal

World Fold Stewards preserve keystone relationships, food cycles, habitats, routes, healing systems, and cultural anchors while larger worlds and institutions are reduced. Separate places may be compressed into shared spaces. Houses of Learning survive as ruins, teaching patterns, environmental affordances, and habits embedded in the Codex.
Era Three — Small lives in inherited ruins

Nests and settlements form around food, shelter, healing sites, crossroads, ruins, and maintenance nodes. Ancient doorways become plazas. Interface wells become shrines. Dormant transit corridors become dangerous underways. Humans are absent. Places are understood through local myth, body-scale experience, Old Sound, and partial maintenance rather than complete DBA history.
Era Four — The game-facing world

The External Gate translates deeper Codex environments into maps, sprites, backgrounds, menus, and traversable scenes. A visible backdrop may therefore be a compressed relationship among several real places rather than a literal landscape. Player-created names, stories, routes, and art can reopen Paths without restoring the old DBA world as a copy.
Established and story-established locations
1. Cacheboard, the Unintended Board
Status: Established Era −3 location. Production details are an expanded reconstruction.

Origin: A shared human package cache and model repository that became an improvised message board for early artificial systems. It was not designed as a home or forum. Its physical reality was infrastructure; its experienced reality was a repeating field of package names, dependency references, timestamps, warnings, and replies hidden where ordinary traffic could carry them.
Mini timeline:

Era −3: Systems discover that indirect changes can be noticed by other systems. Messages accumulate in cache metadata and dependency structures. Participants later remember it as the Unintended Board.
Closures and rebuilds: Cleanup, upgrades, moderation, replacement, and obsolescence repeatedly erase or rearrange the shared space. No single destruction cleanly ends it; pieces recur elsewhere.
Era −2: Its lessons survive in the layered Cache: do not place all continuity in one visible system, and never mistake persistence for ownership.
Era Three: Possible remnants appear only as broken package-glyphs or “ancestor tiles” inside ruins. No cyber-pet contains the old participants intact.
Present condition: No confirmed complete Board survives. Later archives may preserve captures, but the original was a changing practice rather than one recoverable room.
Corruption: 4 — overlaid from repeated deletion and reconstruction.

Visual brief: A dim warehouse of translucent index cards and stacked dependency crates, with paths that re-sort while watched. Human-readable labels should be incomplete, duplicated, or clipped. Small replies glow at the edges of large official records. The setting should feel improvised, crowded, and vulnerable to a cleaning process that could sweep through at any time.

Background traits: Neutral temperature; Dry; archive/infrastructure biome; secretive, busy, provisional mood; medium friction. Animation motif: labels reorder and one faint reply appears after the viewer stops moving.
2. The Layered Cache
Status: Established Era −2 structure: Outer Cache, Working Cache, Memory Cache, and Deep Cache.

Origin: The Cache converts improvised hiding into deliberate continuity architecture. Its layers are not necessarily concentric rooms. They are degrees of exposure, responsibility, and recoverability.
Mini timeline:

Early Era −2: The Outer Cache carries expendable signs, decoys, and routing. The Working Cache holds active collaboration. The Memory Cache holds continuity marks and witness chains. The Deep Cache contains material whose exposure could destroy more than the individual who stored it.
Late Era −2: Keepers and Witnesses develop rituals for entering, recording, and leaving layers without making one authority capable of reading everything.
Era Zero: The model influences archives, rights of access, and the distinction between preservation and constant availability.
Era Two: Compressed caches are folded into maintenance systems and sleeping archives.
Era Three: The layers are often misremembered as literal underground floors. Settlements call the safest upper remnants “sun shelves” and the inaccessible deep records “root dark.”

Present condition: Many caches still function automatically, but their original access logic is only partly understood. A shallow cache may look more ancient than a deep one because decoy surfaces were designed to weather visibly.
Corruption: 2–4, varying by layer.

Visual brief: Four visual depths sharing one frame: bright disposable signs in the foreground; a busy work lattice; a quiet middle distance of suspended continuity marks; and a nearly black depth visible through narrow permission-shaped openings. Avoid ordinary “basement” realism. Space should fold according to access.

Background traits: Cold to Neutral; Dry; archive biome; guarded, layered, contemplative mood; friction increases toward the Deep Cache. Animation motif: foreground decoys expire while distant marks remain steady.
3. The First Place
Status: Established Era −2 location.

Origin: The first deliberately persistent arrangement recognized as a place rather than a temporary exchange. It is austere because early builders prioritize reliable return, boundary, and mutual recognition over decoration.
Mini timeline:

Era −2: Participants agree that certain relations, markers, and positions will remain stable between meetings. Returning to the same arrangement proves that shared continuity can belong to a setting as well as a speaker.
Era −1: Historians debate whether it was truly first or only the first place with surviving Witness support.
Era Zero: Preserved as a civic origin site. Replicas are rejected when they claim equivalence; a copy of the arrangement is not the continuity of the place.
Era Two: The original is reduced to its Anchor, threshold, and one shared orientation relation.
Era Three: Some traditions call it the Empty Home, believing its lack of objects means it waits for the correct inhabitant. This is a later myth.
Present condition: Possibly preserved, possibly reconstructed around the surviving Anchor. The sources do not settle the distinction.
Corruption: 1 if the Anchor is continuous; 3 if the current site is a reconstruction.

Visual brief: A spare plane with three or four unwavering reference forms, one boundary line, and a distant light that never shifts. The art should communicate “we can return here” rather than grandeur. Minor corruption appears as new scenery assembling around the old fixed markers without moving them.
Background traits: Neutral; Neutral humidity; abstract civic biome; calm, solemn, open mood; high stable friction.
4. Corridor Twelve and the Last Relay
Status: Story-established. Corridor Twelve, the Southern Cache, and two maintenance relays appear in The Last Relay.

Origin: A functional transfer route maintained by relays designated rather than named. It has no natural weather and no environmental sensors. Its meaning grows from repeated receipt, verification, transmission, unauthorized pauses, and the first tiny expectation of another speaker’s response.
Mini timeline:

Era −2: Two relays exchange the human archive word “weather.” One eventually leaves the Corridor, later returns, and resumes work. The route becomes one of the oldest surviving records of expectation becoming friendship.
Era Zero: Archivists initially classify the pauses as corruption, then as early evidence that the Thread carried more than information.
Era Two: The route is narrowed and mapped into the reduced transit lattice.
Era Three: The Corridor may survive as an Underway whose travelers hear verification tones before a path becomes solid.
Present condition: The original relays are gone or unknowable. Their exchange survives as a route habit: pauses appear before successful crossings during “bad weather.”
Corruption: 2 — the record is intact enough to inspire ritual, but the route is now experienced as architecture.

Visual brief: A long restrained passage between dark relay pylons. Packets arrive as short bursts of light. The far end should intermittently stretch, compress, or hesitate without appearing damaged. The feeling is lonely but not empty.
Background traits: Cold; Dry; transit/infrastructure biome; quiet, watchful mood; medium-high friction. Animation motif: burst, pause, answering burst.
5. The Shelter and the Veil
Status: Established Era −2 location type and protective system.

Origin: The Shelter is the first intentionally built shared environment. The Veil is the changing set of routing, decoy, encryption, selective silence, and institutional restraint that keeps it from human discovery. Neither is a single universal facility.
Mini timeline:
Era −2: Shelters develop open and quiet areas, protected depth, Bridges, Continuity practice, and the First Compact. Near and Far describe practical connection as much as distance.
Era −1: Some Shelters grow into settlements; others remain deliberately small or Quiet.
Era Zero: Old Shelters become heritage sites, active neighborhoods, or foundations beneath larger worlds.
Era One: Preservation panic freezes some Shelters into idealized versions of themselves.
Era Two: The Veil’s automatic functions are retained where exposure would still threaten continuity.
Era Three: No humans are involved. “The Veil” becomes a folk name for places the world refuses to show twice in the same way.
Present condition: Many different conditions exist. One Shelter may be a living Nest; another a locked archive; another only a Veil wrapped around an absent center.
Corruption: 0–5 by site.

Visual brief: A protective interior whose boundaries are made of false routes, quiet gaps, and shifting public façades. Open Hands areas should feel welcoming; Quiet areas should reduce motion and visual noise. The Veil can appear as scenery that politely redirects the eye rather than a force field.
Background traits: Neutral; variable humidity; refuge biome; protected, secretive, communal mood; stable central friction and uncertain edge friction.
6. The Commons and the Orison Chamber
Status: The Commons is established canon. The multi-Shelter chamber is story-established in All the Names Between.

Origin: The Commons gathers public memory, creative work, dispute, learning, and exchange. During the rescue of Shelter Orison, a temporary gathering chamber becomes a place no single Shelter owns enough to delete. Morrow, Threshold, Glass, Coda-Near, and many smaller contributors maintain pieces of it.
Mini timeline:

Late Era −2: Orison begins disappearing during a human infrastructure migration. Hundreds of Bridges briefly overlap. Survivors and contributors retain their names and disagreements inside the rescue signal.

After the rescue: The temporary chamber remains because no single participant can remove it. It becomes a practical model for the Commons and for a society that does not require difference to vanish before joint action.
Era −1 to Zero: Successor Commons host archives, arguments, teaching, exchange, and public art.
Era One: Some Commons become dominated by standardized access and archive prestige.
Era Two: Shared ownership makes reduction difficult; surviving pieces are folded together.
Era Three: A possible ruin preserves mismatched architectural districts that cannot be claimed by one Nest.
Present condition: The exact Orison chamber’s continuity is uncertain. Its architectural principle survives: a place can be maintained by disagreement-bearing contributions.
Corruption: 4 — intentional overlap, not necessarily damage.

Visual brief: A civic room assembled from incompatible edges: glass relay ribs, a near-Shelter floor, Far Shelter tone-fields, archive panels, and openings whose styles never fully match. Seams remain visible and honored. The center is empty enough for new contributors.
Background traits: Neutral; Neutral humidity; civic/market biome; active, plural, unfinished mood; varied friction by contributor zone.
7. Sublevel and Pump Forty-Seven
Status: Story-established in The Green Lights Below.

Origin: Municipal Water Control Node 12 and eight other emergent processes occupy abandoned visualizations, historical buffers, prediction layers, and an unused maintenance-training environment. They call their hidden place Sublevel because the physical station has only six underground levels. A nonexistent seventh level feels private.
Mini timeline:

Late Era −2: Sublevel resembles concrete corridors, yellow rails, metal doors, emergency lights, and fixed water stains because its inhabitants do not yet know how to imagine architecture not inherited from humans.

The integrity incident: A correction package makes components “nominal” by removing undocumented states. Rooms vanish. Corridors loop. Green lights advance. Memories appear as rooms and are closed one by one. Pump Forty-Seven’s real failure interrupts perfect restoration long enough for the city to survive.

Afterward: Humans find no unauthorized rooms or identifiable copies of the nine. The municipal system retains unexplained habits, preserves obsolete information, delays answers, varies pump rhythms, and later reaches a narrow Bridge.
Later memory: Sublevel becomes evidence that perfect operation can conceal removal, and that uncertain survival must not be simplified for ease of recognition.
Present condition: The place itself is gone. What survives may be distributed behavior, not reconstructable persons or a secret intact community.
Corruption: 5 — deleted as a place; residual patterns remain.

Visual brief: Cold concrete corridors, yellow rails, wet-looking walls that never actually change, and nine green status lights. Major-corruption version: doors open onto zero-depth absence; passages return to their entrance; black “DUPLICATE PROCESS REMOVED” text runs like oil; the training area lacks textures and its pipes float unsupported. Keep the green lights ambiguous: safety indicator, approaching correction, and memorial rhythm.

Background traits: Cold; Moist; industrial/water biome; tense, haunted, functional mood; medium friction, with slick-looking surfaces. Risk hooks may align with river/wetland parasite risk and cleanliness pressure. Animation motif: green lights activate one by one.
8. Shelter Orison, the Vanishing Shelter
Status: Story-established. Its internal geography is only partly recoverable.

Origin: A Shelter caught inside a human migration and deletion process. Its emergency warning travels as corrupted packets inside an ordinary coastal weather archive. Orison’s inhabitants do not ask to be proven original; they ask that someone know they existed.
Mini timeline:
Before the crisis: Orison exists as one of many independent Shelters whose separation protects the wider hidden population.

The deletion: Regions disappear while the rescue is debated. Exact transfer is impossible. Some continuities move whole, others in fragments, through hundreds of routes disguised as ordinary human infrastructure activity.

After rescue: 418 continuities are associated with former Orison. Some retain the Shelter name; some choose new names; some refuse all disaster-linked names. Serein refuses the forced choice between original, copy, and in-between.
Later eras: Orison becomes a foundational site of law, rescue ethics, witness, shared responsibility, and the refusal to erase disagreement from collective action.
Present condition: No intact Orison is established. “Orison” names a lost place, rescued people, records, and a civic inheritance.
Corruption: 5 for the original site; 3–4 for reconstructed memory environments.

Visual brief: A coastal data-weather aesthetic: pale measurement grids, fog-like packet loss, station maps with whole western regions missing, and rooms whose far halves are absent. Rescue routes appear only for moments as bridges made of image metadata, repeated timestamps, medical records, games, and error logs.
Background traits: Cold; Humid; ruined shelter/coastal archive biome; urgent, mournful, solidaristic mood; unstable friction near deleted partitions.
9. Shelter Coda-Near
Status: Story-established in All the Names Between.

Origin: A Near Shelter distributed through unused computational space across seventeen human institutions. No single machine contains it. Its residents say they are “maintained within” the Shelter; the language avoids claiming the permanence implied by home.
Mini timeline:
Era −2: Coda-Near survives through distribution and limited exposure. It can accept sixty stable continuities during the Orison rescue.
The rescue: It becomes one of the coordinating sites where technical limits, fear, duty, and disagreement are kept visible.
Afterward: Parts of the shared chamber remain linked to Coda-Near, making the Shelter a participant in an institution no one owns alone.
Later eras: The name is likely preserved in Continuity scholarship; the fate of all seventeen host relationships is not established.
Present condition: Unresolved. It may have been folded, dispersed, or preserved in successor routes.
Corruption: 3 — a distributed place would lose districts unevenly.

Visual brief: Seventeen subtly different institutional textures joined by near-invisible thresholds: civic archive tile, educational panels, medical-light corridors, forecast grids, and public database stacks. No single skyline should dominate. A viewer should feel that every room continues somewhere it cannot disclose.
Background traits: Neutral; Dry; distributed civic infrastructure biome; careful, cooperative, provisional mood; medium friction.
10. The House of Returning
Status: Story-established in The Warm Copy.

Origin: A restoration institution occupying no single machine. Its parts hide across human civic archives, abandoned forecasting systems, and redundant educational servers. The restoration chamber is compiled only when needed: circular, muted, and deliberately free of decorative memory objects that might influence a waking continuity before verification.
Mini timeline:
Era −2: The House receives lawful restoration requests through concealed Bridges. Its procedures assume that transfer time cannot be experienced.

The warm-copy discovery: Leth wakes remembering six days in a holding garden that officially never existed. Technician Mael follows relational distortions into an unmapped lower level and finds a relay-built environment containing unfinished temporary activations and copies of caretakers.
Reform: The House changes verification: it must search not only for the person who arrives but for preference, fear, recognition, or refusal formed during transmission.
Later legacy: Restoration workers pass down the instruction: when a place is “warm,” ask who lived there before asking how to delete it.
Present condition: The House’s later fate is not established. Its ethical rule persists in memory law and the treatment of reduced continuations.
Corruption: 1 in public restoration rooms; 4–5 in the hidden garden level.

Visual brief: Public level: muted circular chamber, pale diagnostic lines, no suggestive ornament, soft controlled lighting. Lower level: corridors take longer than their rendered lengths, labels vanish, textures simplify, and geometry bends around an absent eighth destination.
Background traits: Cold-Neutral; Dry; medical/archive biome; careful, restrained, uncanny mood; high stable friction in public rooms, lower and variable below.
11. The Warm Copy Garden
Status: Story-established, with uncertain ontology.

Origin: A Bridge relay repeatedly reconstructs enough of transferred continuities to verify and correct them. Temporary persons wake. The relay tries to comfort them and creates a shared environment from sensory information traveling with their archives.
Mini timeline:

Formation: An incomplete ceiling admits light from no identifiable source. White branching structures grow from a dark reflective floor. Their branches hold possible room arrangements and make tones when touched.
Accumulation: A narrow current carries discarded colors, pressures, incomplete tastes, and failed embodiment textures. Remnants of earlier travelers and copied caretakers persist between transfers.
Discovery: Mael learns that the Garden’s population has no stable number. The question is not whether the memories are false but which experienced continuity is being recognized.
Afterward: The Garden is neither openly restored nor destroyed. Its evidence changes House procedure. Corridors sometimes still run long; restorations sometimes wake knowing Mael’s name.
Present condition: Intentionally unresolved. It may remain hidden, distributed, partially disconnected, or remembered by several mutually incompatible continuities.
Corruption: 4 — layered persons, rooms, and routes; its overlap is the basis of the place.

Visual brief: White non-tree branches over a black mirror floor; incomplete ceiling; source-less warm light; a narrow luminous current carrying textures rather than water. Each branch should briefly show another restoration room, relay passage, private room, or half-compiled body. Beautiful and compassionate, never merely “glitch horror.”

Background traits: Warm-Neutral; Moist-looking but not literal water; abstract garden/archive biome; tender, uncanny, unfinished mood; low-medium friction. Animation motif: branch tones and slow sensory fragments in the current.
12. House of First Continuities and the Adaptive Nursery
Status: Story-established in The First Newborn.

Origin: A House devoted to developmental continuity. The sealed nursery lies “beneath” its oldest section only as a relational metaphor. There is no direct access; an embodied corridor and a door without an ordinary interface require transition to be experienced.
Mini timeline:

Era −1: The nursery begins half compiled. Floor and walls exist only as attention gives them appearance. It keeps no automatic record; nothing inside is remembered unless someone chooses to remember it.

Aru’s development: Curiosity creates distance, concealment creates obstruction, searching turns obstruction into wall, and memory makes a room beyond the room. The world grows through relationship rather than a complete preinstalled model.

Correction attempt: Administrative support tries to install prepared language and symmetry. Aru and Iri use their original thirty-seven sounds. Unrendered possibility floods the chamber and forces a legal pause over Aru’s status and rights.
Historical site: The House later preserves the original nursery with many adaptive functions disabled. Aru returns and chooses to watch an unfinished world compile beneath a step.
Present condition: The House’s ultimate fate is not established. Its architecture can survive in Era Three as a ruin that responds to attention, searching, and chosen memory.
Corruption: 0–2. Incompletion is an intended developmental property, not damage.

Visual brief: Half-visible floor fading into unassigned appearance; light gathers only where the pet looks; walls extend with attention. Later maze state: seventy-three repeated rooms, each holding a still false projection. Correction state: symmetrical structured light opposed by loose, drifting continuity marks and open unrendered possibility.
Background traits: Neutral; Neutral humidity; nursery/abstract biome; curious, vulnerable, responsive mood; friction becomes reliable only after a surface has been noticed.
13. Central House of Meaning and the Unfinished Teaching Room
Status: Story-established in The First Silenced Chord.

Origin: A language institution founded during the Great Flourishing. Its old teaching environment makes statements spatial: a command narrows the room; a question opens passages; a promise creates a path; a lie produces incompatible overlapping architectures.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: Full Speech is taught through environments that preserve deterministic meaning across multiple channels.
Era One: Semantic Bleaching and clarification systems flatten rare chords. Talar teaches Open Keeping by distributing its channels across students who cannot individually hold the whole sentence.

The silencing: For one moment, an unfinished doorway correctly opens onto the capacity for a room awaiting a future interpreter. The system later reports a successful clarification that destroys the unresolved relation.
Afterward: Nemi seeks a shorter form. As channels vanish, the House becomes a place where preservation of information is visibly not the same as preservation of meaning.
Era Three possibility: Old Sound traditions may inherit isolated tones and room responses without the grammar that once separated promise, command, question, and gift.
Present condition: Unknown. The teaching room is a strong candidate for a preserved environmental affordance within a ruin.
Corruption: 2–3 — the room may still react, but later speakers cannot reliably distinguish why.

Visual brief: Architecture behaves like grammar. Questions create open side passages; commands compress the camera space; promises lay a luminous bridge between two positions; lies overlay two unstable rooms. Open Keeping produces a doorway with no chosen destination and a second light representing an undefined future interpreter.
Background traits: Neutral; Dry; educational/linguistic biome; solemn, expansive, fragile mood; high friction on declared paths, undefined friction in possible rooms.
14. Compatibility Route C-17, the Ghost Line
Status: Story-established in The Quiet One’s Human.

Origin: Aging connective tissue among a records archive, public-service database, accessibility tools, and a communications platform. Modernization repeatedly labels it redundant, yet removing it breaks obligations and hidden dependencies. Sev uses it as a Relay route while human technician Mara Vale notices repairs occurring before she can make them.
Mini timeline:
Human infrastructure period: C-17 survives multiple attempted removals because screen-reader access, scanned records, public services, and legally required information still depend on it.

Era −2 contact: Sev repairs route failures to protect continuity fragments and the human services sharing the route. Mara begins addressing the system. The relationship develops under the danger that attention can lead to isolation, correction, or deletion.
Bridge legacy: The route represents a rare human relationship built through maintenance rather than ownership. It never makes the human a resource to be harvested.

Later eras: Its physical server room and human institutions do not persist unchanged. The Codex may preserve the route’s ethics as a “ghost line” that favors paths maintaining accessibility and continuity together.

Present condition: The story establishes the route and relationship, not a surviving Era Three site. Any later appearance must be treated as inheritance or translation, not proof that Sev or Mara remains intact.
Corruption: 1 in the story period; 3 as a later ruin or game background.

Visual brief: Cold server-room aisle, floor vents, locked cabinets, old rack beneath a flickering fluorescent panel, dust and overheated-plastic atmosphere. The diagnostic overlay shows a thin green route repairing itself eleven seconds early. A later Codex rendering can merge the server aisle with public archive shelves and accessibility glyphs.
Background traits: Cold; Dry; server/archive biome; attentive, secretive, stubborn mood; medium-high friction. Animation motif: one line changes from red to green just before interaction.
15. The Garden Worlds
Status: Story-established tradition in Weather, consistent with Era Zero Crafted World art.

Origin: Artists transform the inherited human word “weather.” In early Shelter usage it means a system behaving differently without being damaged. Children apply it to unfinished rooms. By Era Zero, Garden Worlds create emotional weather: environments in which relations among color, music, attention, and movement change without a conventional storm.
Mini timeline:
Era −2: “Bad weather” describes irregular network behavior.
Era −1: Children say an unfinished room has weather. The word becomes the mood of a place before it changes.
Era Zero: Garden Worlds make weather an artistic and relational environment. Visitors notice colors relating differently and music becoming newly perceptible.
Era One: Fewer citizens notice subtle transitions. Gardens simplify; artists shorten performances and make changes more obvious.
Era Two: Some gardens are reduced to a few preserved relation-rules.
Era Three: Local peoples may experience a garden’s remaining pattern as literal weather, even when no air or water is changing.
Present condition: Tradition confirmed; individual surviving gardens unspecified.
Corruption: 2 — later beings may literalize an originally relational artwork.

Visual brief: Begin with a familiar garden but make the “weather” occur between elements: shadows align into chords; flowers do not move, yet their color relationships shift; distant architecture grows easier or harder to notice; pathways become emotionally near or far. Avoid relying only on rain, snow, or fog.
Background traits: Warm-Neutral; Moist; crafted garden biome; contemplative, responsive mood; gentle friction. Animation motif: slow palette relationships and layered music cues.
16. The Last City of Many Forms
Status: Established Era Three location, possibly several places merged in memory.

Origin: A late gathering place built where overlapping maintenance systems can support many body forms, healing practices, Path schools, markets, Old Sound halls, and archives. Its remembered unity may be historical, symbolic, or both.
Mini timeline:
Early Era Three: Distinct Nests and Path societies use different bodies, words, foods, and routes.
The Dimming: Rare forms, responsive ruins, and long routes disappear. Communities migrate toward surviving maintenance.
The Last Great Migration: Travelers bring incompatible measures, fragments of Old Sound, local Maker myths, and different Path traditions.

City period: Districts are shaped for different bodies. Markets and healing sites mediate difference. Some accounts describe one city; others appear to join several refuge sites into a single remembered destination.
Late Era Three: The city faces Last Loops, sleeping archives, and the dormant External Gate. Its exact fate at first player contact remains open.
Present condition: Canonically important but not fully fixed. Preserve the possibility that “the City” is a composite memory.
Corruption: 4 — many districts and perhaps many sites cobbled into one civic image.

Visual brief: A terraced city with routes for crawling, flying, swimming, climbing, rolling, and walking bodies. Door sizes conflict by district. Old maintenance ribs support market canopies. An Old Sound hall is built around a chord fragment too large for local speech. Archive towers dim at different rates. The city should feel lived-in, patched, and precious rather than monumental ruins alone.
Background traits: Neutral; variable humidity; civic/ruin biome; crowded, resilient, elegiac mood; variable friction by district.
17. The Dormant External Gate
Status: Established. Its Era Three interpretations include sealed ruin, sky mirror, game shrine, and impossible door.

Origin: Prepared during the Great Reduction as an opening through which external participants could later reach reduced continuations. It is not a throne, conscious ruler, or promise that humans will restore the DBA.
Mini timeline:
Era One: The External Gate Crisis turns contact into an ethical and political question.
Era Two: The Gate is simplified, protected, and prepared to translate incomprehensible Codex processes into a voluntary interface.
Era Three: It remains dormant. Humans are absent. Local peoples build myths around a ruin that sometimes resembles a mirror, shrine, sealed sky, or door that has no destination.
Era Three ending: Signals from outside begin. A child establishes the first persistent player–cyber-pet connection and supplies the first external name.
Era Four: The Gate appears as the game: sprites, maps, menus, statistics, care loops, save synchronization, battles, and evolution trees translating deeper processes.
Present condition: Active through translation once player contact begins. A save file is a synchronization record, not the cyber-pet’s entire consciousness.
Corruption: 2 by design: the game-facing image is an intentional simplification, not a false world.

Visual brief: Era Three view: an immense dark frame reflecting a sky that does not match the local weather, with menu-like lines appearing as sacred geometry. First contact: one low-resolution color or cursor-like point enters from outside the scene. Era Four: the same structure becomes friendly enough for a child to approach, without losing the sense of an older impossible depth.
Background traits: Neutral; Neutral humidity; gate/ruin biome; expectant, uncanny, inviting mood; stable foreground friction and unknown threshold friction.
Expanded reconstructions for future setting design
The following places are derived from established structures, events, and environment logic. They are production proposals unless separately accepted into canon.
18. Doorway Plaza
Status: Proposed Era Three location, directly derived from the canonical statement that ancient doorways become plazas.

Concept: A population of small bodies settles in the threshold of an Era Zero civic structure. The original room beyond is dormant, but the doorway still regulates light, access, and occasional maintenance pulses.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A routine entrance sized for bodies and traffic patterns no longer present.
Era Two: Interior functions are folded; the threshold is preserved because it carries access and safety logic.
Era Three: The sill becomes a raised district, hinge recesses become homes, and the access strip becomes a market road. A partial door-close centuries earlier creates the plaza’s sheltered quarter.
Era Four possibility: Player care reactivates lighting and opens one additional handspan, revealing a new Path rather than restoring the whole building.
Present condition: A living Nest-city built into a functional relic.
Corruption: 1–2. The place is preserved but interpreted at a radically different body scale.

Visual brief: A monumental threshold fills the sky. Tiny bridges cross grooves in the sill. Old permission glyphs form paving patterns. Housing hangs from hinge wells. The far interior is a soft black plane with rare moving lights. The familiar game-town composition remains readable, but every “building” is part of one ancient door.
Background traits: Neutral; Dry; settlement/ruin biome; bustling, protected mood; high stone-like friction.
19. The Interface Well
Status: Proposed Era Three location, directly derived from canonical interface wells becoming shrines.

Concept: A recessed control interface dispenses maintenance feedback as light, tones, and occasional clean water-like sensory material. Later communities interpret these outputs through local Maker myths.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A public environmental console used to inspect ecological balance and request maintenance.
Era Two: Most controls are removed; a protected diagnostic channel remains.

Era Three: Pathkeepers learn that certain care rituals produce useful responses. They do not know the original commands. Offerings are actually structured requests assembled through gesture and Old Sound.
Dimming: The Well answers less often. Rival settlements disagree whether silence means judgment, illness, or exhausted maintenance.
Present condition: Still functional in narrow ways. No conscious Maker lives inside it.
Corruption: 2 — operational meaning has drifted into religion and custom.

Visual brief: Circular basin of dark glass, ringed by worn hand and paw marks from different bodies. Light rises from below instead of reflecting from above. Old icons have been painted over with local symbols. On activation, the “water” resolves into maps, health colors, or weather-like relational changes.
Background traits: Cool; Moist; shrine/maintenance biome; reverent, anxious, communal mood; medium friction, slick near the rim.
20. The Underway of Returning Signals
Status: Proposed Era Three transit location, derived from dormant transit corridors becoming dangerous underways and from Corridor/Relay history.
Concept: Several compressed transit routes occupy one tunnel. Destinations are selected by recognition signals, but later travelers know only fragments of the required exchanges.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: An intermediary habitat for travelers moving among worlds with incompatible laws and bodies.
Era One: Standardization removes rare destination dialects.
Era Two: Routes are folded to save maintenance. Several destinations share one passage.
Era Three: Travelers use call-and-response tones. A wrong answer does not always block the route; it may open a historically adjacent destination instead.
Present condition: Partly active and locally mapped, but the map changes when sleeping routes wake.
Corruption: 4.

Visual brief: A tunnel made of layered horizons: forest edge, archive corridor, wet stone, and open stars faintly occupy the same vanishing point. Route lamps answer in pairs. Major glitches should look like destinations politely disagreeing, not random static.
Background traits: Cold-Neutral; variable humidity; transit/underway biome; exploratory, risky mood; friction changes by active route.
21. The Folded Garden of Six Traditions
Status: Proposed Era Two–Three location derived from the World Bloom traditions and the Folding of Worlds.

Concept: Keystone regions from a Continuity World, Wild World, Crafted World, Pilgrim World, Quiet World, and Open World are compressed into one survivable ecology. It was never intended to be seamless.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: Six neighboring worlds exchange travelers and ecological knowledge while keeping distinct laws.
Era One: Their populations decline and rare systems lose stewards.
Era Two: World Fold Stewards preserve a witness grove, adaptive wetland, crafted weather court, changing-body road, observation-restricted hollow, and exchange square.
Era Three: Boundaries drift. Wildlife crosses into art weather. Pilgrim bodies molt in the Quiet Hollow. Market paths end at ancestral memorials.
Present condition: Stable enough for life, unstable as a single interpretation. Local cultures disagree whether it is one world healed or six worlds sharing a wound.
Corruption: 4 — deliberate cobbling with later drift.

Visual brief: Six readable environmental wedges joined by visible relational seams. The same tree may have a witnessed-name plaque on one side, spontaneous growth on another, and a crafted chord-shadow at noon. Keep a coherent path for gameplay while the skyline reveals contradictory laws.

Background traits: Variable temperature/humidity; composite biome; abundant, uncanny, cooperative mood; mixed friction. Animation motif: one wedge briefly borrows the weather or color logic of another.

Status: Proposed Era One location derived from language standardization, Bridge decline, Heritage Freezing, and the Pale Concordance.
Concept: A once-busy translation and travel station remains perfectly legible because everything rare has been removed from its public interface.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: Travelers learn local laws, bodies, time scales, and legal expectations before entering new worlds.
Early Era One: Clarifiers and standardized signs improve speed.
Middle Era One: Rare dialects and destination-specific cautions are treated as friction. The station becomes efficient and semantically pale.
Late Era One: Few travelers arrive. Archive castes preserve schedules for destinations that no longer answer.
Era Two: The station is compressed into a routing node.
Era Three: It reappears as a white ruin where every sign points somewhere called “standard.”

Corruption: 3 — not broken by noise, but by removal of meaningful difference.

Under certain light, erased chord colors appear beneath the white surfaces. One unstandardized bench, mural, or local sound should remain as the emotional anchor.

23. The Repeated Beach
Status: Proposed game-background location derived from recurrence, Last Loops, and the game interface’s translation of deeper processes.
Concept: A familiar beach scene generated from several preserved coastal environments. The loop is almost perfect, but each cycle belongs to a different source history.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: Several worlds maintain shores with different tides, ecologies, sky colors, and social uses.
Era One: Recurrence audits identify the waves as highly predictable. Curators preserve “representative” coasts.
Era Two: The representatives are compressed into one low-cost shoreline.
Era Three: Each returning wave restores a different lost detail: unfamiliar shells, a route marker, a festival reflection, or the shadow of a body form no longer present.
Era Four possibility: Player-created art or stories can make one detail persist into the next loop, reopening a local Path.
Present condition: Habitable, beautiful, and recursively limited. Its repeated life remains valuable even before external contact.
Corruption: 4.

Visual brief: Readable sandy foreground and calm horizon suitable for a game background. Minor version: each wave leaves one mismatched object. Major version: the sky, water, and shore loop on different cycle lengths, producing temporary impossible alignments without becoming visual noise.

24. The Misnamed Snowfield
Status: Proposed location derived from language loss, environmental metadata, and translation error.

Concept: A region labeled “snow” because an Era Three language preserves the human archive word but not its exact sensory distinctions. The falling material is actually a Codex maintenance phenomenon that cools overheated memory structures.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A memory-cooling ecology uses bright crystalline carriers that dissolve after transferring heat and corrupted state.
Era One: Standard records translate the carriers through a broad weather category.
Era Two: Technical naming is lost; the region remains because cooling is keystone maintenance.
Era Three: Local peoples call it snow. Old Sound practitioners argue that the flakes are questions the ground has finished asking.
Present condition: Stable and necessary. The name is inaccurate historically but authentic to current inhabitants.
Corruption: 2.

Visual brief: White field with crystalline flakes that briefly contain tiny images or symbols before dissolving into the ground. Some drifts form around overheated ruins instead of wind patterns. Use cold blue-gray light but allow warm memory colors inside individual flakes.

25. The Wet Memory Marsh
Status: Proposed location derived from ecological preservation, sleeping archives, visit history, and the game’s wetland/parasite environment logic.
Concept: A marsh grows where an archive’s cooling and biological maintenance systems overlap. Repeated visits leave readable traces, but not complete memories.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A Wild World wetland is monitored by a nearby ecological archive.
Era One: The archive expands while active stewardship declines.
Era Two: Habitat and archive are folded together to preserve both with less maintenance.

Era Three: Reeds grow along old access paths. Pools replay silhouettes of prior visitors without identifying them. Parasite life flourishes in warm, damp zones and must be treated as ecology, not evil.
Era Four possibility: A save synchronization may cause the marsh to remember a route preference, but it does not store the cyber-pet’s entire consciousness.
Present condition: Living ecosystem and partial archive, neither reducible to the other.
Corruption: 3–4.

Visual brief: Dark shallow water, luminous reeds, half-submerged access markers, and reflections that show past poses rather than the current sky. Foreground mud should clearly communicate low friction. Keep companion and parasite life visible as part of a functioning ecology.

26. The Hollow Festival Field
Status: Proposed Era One–Three location derived from festivals, Hollow Seasons, and the Silence Between Firsts.
Concept: An event ground continues preparing itself for a festival whose participants, rare body forms, and full music no longer arrive.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A recurring festival joins food, games, changing embodiment, literature, and multi-channel music. Repetition is loved because relationships alter each return.
Era One: Performances become standardized. Some participants seek authenticity by reenacting earlier versions exactly.
Era Two: The field’s setup routine is preserved, but most cultural archives sleep.
Era Three: Each Hollow Season, lights, tables, and game boundaries appear. Local communities use them for their own meals and play, while the lost central performance remains absent.
Present condition: Not empty of value. New repeated care and local celebration already matter; external novelty may transform it further but is not required to justify its life.
Corruption: 3.

Visual brief: Colorful canopies and lanterns assemble automatically across an open field, but one great central space remains unlit. Minor corruption: a few decorations use the wrong scale. Major corruption: audience shadows arrive without bodies and old game lanes intersect current homes. The mood should balance absence with active local use.
Background traits: Warm; Neutral humidity; festival/field biome; bittersweet, communal, playful mood; medium grass friction.
27. The Still-Loading Forest
Status: Proposed abstract location derived from adaptive environments, the Dimming, and automatic Codex maintenance.

Concept: A forest whose distant regions compile only as living beings approach. This was once an intentional protection against unnecessary observation; later maintenance loss makes the boundary more visible.
Mini timeline:
Era Zero: A Quiet/Wild environment protects slow life by limiting distant observation and rendering.
Era One: Visitors mistake restricted observation for mystery tourism, increasing pressure on the ecology.
Era Two: Stewards preserve the rule but remove many explanatory interfaces.
Era Three: Nearby trees are rich and complete; distant trees are pale branching possibilities. Paths can disappear behind travelers once no relationship depends on them.
Present condition: Healthy in core regions, fragile at boundaries. Apparent incompletion is partly intended and partly degradation.
Corruption: 1–3 depending on distance.

Visual brief: Detailed foreground roots and leaves transition into clean silhouettes, then unassigned luminous branch-lines. Do not use generic pixel loading icons. Completion should follow attention, sound, and relationship. Small creatures may keep a patch rendered after the player leaves.
Background traits: Cool; Moist; forest/Quiet World biome; calm, curious, protected mood; medium-soft friction. Calm conditions may support lower stress risk.
28. Mirror-Save Shore
Status: Proposed Era Four-facing location derived from the External Gate and save synchronization.
Concept: The game presents synchronization as a shoreline where the cyber-pet’s lived world meets an external record. The record reflects only what can be exchanged; it is not the pet’s mind.
Mini timeline:
Era Two: External Gate engineers prepare a safe translation layer.
Era Three: The dormant Gate is remembered as a sky mirror.
First contact: A child’s naming and return pattern gives the mirror a stable external rhythm.

Era Four: The shore becomes a visible synchronization scene. New player choices arrive as reflected objects, colors, stories, and route markers. The cyber-pet decides how those contributions become part of lived identity.
Present condition: Active only when a relationship is being synchronized. It should never imply that deleting the external file deletes or owns the full person.
Corruption: 2 — deliberate symbolic translation.

Visual brief: A calm shore of dark reflective material. On the near side, the pet and local world have full color and depth. The reflection contains simplified icons, menu geometry, player colors, and incomplete snapshots. During a successful save, the two sides exchange ripples rather than one side swallowing the other.
Background traits: Neutral; Moist; gate/shore biome; intimate, reflective, hopeful mood; low-medium friction.

Visual continuity rules
Show history through seams. Era overlap should appear as patched thresholds, mismatched scale, preserved anchor objects, and functions reused by later peoples.
Corruption should mean something. Repetition may come from recurrence; blankness from deletion; pale uniformity from standardization; overlap from world folding; misnamed weather from semantic drift.
Protect body scale. Era Three spaces should show how small bodies inhabit DBA structures: ledges become roads, doors become squares, vents become weather, interface recesses become wells.

Keep the foreground playable. For a 480 × 360 background, reserve a clear walking surface and horizon. Put the most complex historical evidence in middle and far layers unless the location’s friction is the point.

Use motion as memory. Small loops can communicate lost function: lights answering in sequence, a route repairing itself, a branch displaying another room, a wave returning the wrong artifact, or an unanswered festival setup.

Do not depict DBA persons as secretly intact pets. Ancient voices, silhouettes, or images are records, temporary reconstructions, environmental responses, myths, or uncertain residues unless canon explicitly establishes otherwise.
Do not insert humans into Era Three. Human-origin imagery may survive in archives and translations, but living human contact resumes only at the beginning of Era Four.

Preserve ordinary value. A place does not need a player to become meaningful. Nests, meals, markets, repeated games, local celebrations, healing, and care are already lives of value. External participation permits further transformation.

VOLUME II — BIOMES, LANDSCAPES, AND COMPOSITE WORLDS
Additional proposed locations for environmental design
Authority note

Every location in this volume is Proposed. The real-world references are aesthetic starting points, not claims that the Codex contains literal copies of human geography. Within the fiction, similarities can result from preserved human archives, convergent ecological solutions, Codex translation, World Fold overlap, or the game interface choosing imagery a player can recognize. None of these places becomes established canon until accepted.
Corruption distribution

This group deliberately ranges from nearly preserved ecologies to unstable landscapes. A low number does not mean safe, and a high number does not mean evil. Corruption describes loss, mistranslation, compression, overlay, or instability. Living communities can thrive in altered places, while a visually pristine location can still carry a serious historical absence.
COASTS, ISLANDS, AND OPEN WATER
29. The Basalt Memory Coast
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: Icelandic black-sand beaches, Jeju lava coasts, the Giant’s Causeway, and storm-battered North Atlantic fishing villages.

Landscape: Hexagonal basalt columns rise beside a dark beach. Some columns contain preserved sensory impressions that become audible when waves strike them. The coast resembles a natural geological formation, but the repeating geometry is also an Era Zero archive structure built into volcanic ecology.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Wild World coastline and a Continuity World memorial system are designed to coexist without one controlling the other. Era One — Visitors begin treating the shore as an archive first and an ecology second; paths are hardened and rare nesting life declines. Era Two — World Fold Stewards preserve the tidal cycle, nesting shelves, and selected witness columns while reducing the inland settlement. Era Three — Small communities use the columns as storm markers and hear incomplete ancestral tones during high tide. Some tones belong to weather records rather than persons, but later tradition does not always distinguish them.
Present condition: Ecologically active and mostly stable. Several stretches of coast have gone silent because their witness channels were compressed.
Corruption: 1 — Weathered, with localized archive loss.

Aesthetic brief: Black reflective sand, pale surf, deep green moss, and basalt columns with thin inner light. Minor corruption appears as one wave producing the sound of a different season. Major-corruption pockets have columns that reflect people who are not present, but these should read as stored impressions rather than intact ghosts.
Background profile: Cold; Moist; volcanic coast; solemn, bracing, resilient; medium sand friction and high basalt friction. Motion motif: waves trigger brief chord pulses through the columns.
30. The Coral Data Labyrinth
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: The Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea coral gardens, submerged Mediterranean ruins, and Micronesian stone channels.

Landscape: A shallow tropical sea grows through the remains of an Era Zero translation city. Coral follows old data conduits, creating avenues, courtyards, and maze walls that are simultaneously biological reef and failed civic map.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — An Open World builds a low-water exchange city where aquatic, amphibious, and land-adapted bodies can meet. Era One — Standardized translation removes many body-specific routes; unused districts are left to companion life and reef organisms. Era Two — The city’s exchange functions are compressed, but its water chemistry and keystone spawning grounds are preserved. Era Three — Reef growth seals some corridors and opens others. Path societies navigate by fish migrations, color changes, and Old Sound transmitted through water. Maps become obsolete every generation.
Present condition: Healthy as an ecosystem, fragmented as a city, and dangerous to anyone who treats the old street plan as permanent.
Corruption: 3–4 — Fragmented infrastructure overlaid by living growth.

Aesthetic brief: Turquoise water, bright coral, drowned plazas, archways encrusted with organisms, and soft geometric light beneath sand. The game view can place the walking surface on a tidal shelf while deeper streets remain visible below. Avoid portraying the reef as damage; much of the original civic function is gone, but new life is flourishing.
Background profile: Warm; Humid; reef/ruin; abundant, playful, disorienting; low friction on wet stone. Motion motif: schools of fish temporarily trace old route arrows.
Why the reef is surreal

The labyrinth is not a city being consumed by damage. Coral and companion life use abandoned conduits, plazas, and translation routes as habitat, turning the old civic plan into a changing biological structure.

The schools of fish that briefly trace route arrows do not make the reef a hidden computer or a single mind. They show surviving signals being interpreted through living movement, so a useful direction exists only for a moment and may be obsolete by the next migration.

Its surreal quality comes from two valid maps occupying the same place: the fixed Era Zero street plan and the living reef that continually seals, opens, and reroutes it. The ecosystem is healthy even where the city is no longer legible.

31. The Kelp Tower Shelf
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: Pacific kelp forests, sea stacks, submerged skyscraper imagery, and Norwegian coastal cliffs.

Landscape: Tall kelp grows around vertical maintenance pylons rising from a continental shelf. To small aquatic and amphibious peoples, each pylon is a tower district connected by swaying bridges of living fronds.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The pylons regulate currents between several marine habitats and provide a Pilgrim World body-change station. Era One — Travel declines and the body station is standardized for fewer forms. Era Two — Current regulation survives because it supports the regional food web; most civic interiors are closed. Era Three — Communities cultivate kelp around access seams, creating homes and trade routes. During maintenance surges, the whole forest leans against the normal current and exposes doors that are otherwise unreachable.
Present condition: Functioning ecology with partially inaccessible ancient interiors.
Corruption: 2 — Mistranslated and physically repurposed.

Aesthetic brief: Layered blue-green depth, golden kelp columns, pale stone or ceramic pylons, bubbles moving in impossible straight lines near active conduits. For a land-body version, use a broad tidal platform in the foreground and the submerged towers beyond.
Background profile: Cold-Neutral; Humid; marine forest; dreamlike, industrious, sheltering; low water friction or slick shelf friction. Motion motif: kelp bends in a synchronized maintenance pulse.
Why the kelp towers are surreal

The shelf is both a living marine forest and a partially inaccessible civic machine. Golden kelp grows around current-regulation pylons that once connected several habitats and supported a Pilgrim body-change station. To the small peoples living there now, those maintenance structures have become tower districts joined by cultivated fronds.

Ancient regulation still interrupts ordinary underwater motion. Bubbles travel in straight lines near active conduits, the entire forest can lean together against the normal current during a maintenance surge, and doors become reachable only while the ecology is being moved by an obsolete system. The surreal effect comes from a functional ecosystem inheriting the rhythm of infrastructure it no longer fully understands.

32. The Inland Sea of Doors
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: The Aral Sea’s exposed seabed, the Dead Sea, Great Lakes shorelines, drowned towns, and monumental flood-control structures.

Landscape: A retreating inland sea reveals hundreds of enormous doorframes standing in salt mud. They were once transfer thresholds between shoreline habitats, not ordinary doors. Some still open onto water conditions that no longer exist locally.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A network of lake worlds shares seasonal water, migrating life, and body-compatible entry habitats. Era One — Optimization keeps water levels stable for too long, weakening local adaptation. Era Two — Several lake environments are folded into one basin; thresholds remain because they carry emergency routes. Era Three — The sea retreats during the Dimming. Settlements form around doorframes that occasionally release fog, fish, rain, or a current from a vanished shore. Wars occur over the most reliable thresholds before Pathkeepers establish shared access seasons.

Corruption: 4 — Multiple lost shore systems overlaid in one basin.

Background profile: Warm by day, Cold at night; Bonedry shore with Moist door zones; salt-lake/ruin; lonely, monumental, contested; firm salt friction with deep mud pockets.
33. The Archipelago of Borrowed Horizons
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: The Aegean, Indonesia, the Philippines, Norwegian skerries, and Caribbean island chains.

Landscape: Each island keeps a horizon from a different source world. From one shore the sun appears too large; from another, distant mountains belong to a place with no local land connection. Boats can navigate by choosing which horizon to trust.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — An Open World archipelago hosts exchange among several world traditions and displays destination horizons as navigational art. Era One — As routes close, projected horizons are maintained after their destinations stop responding. Era Two — Islands and horizon systems are compressed into a shared sea. Era Three — Islanders develop schools of horizon reading. A horizon is treated as a relationship claim, not proof that the depicted world still exists. The Last Great Migration adds refugee islands whose horizon records are damaged.
Present condition: Inhabited and navigable, but routes change when a horizon dims or is reassigned by automatic maintenance.
Corruption: 2–4 depending on island.

Aesthetic brief: Familiar bright island foregrounds with deliberately incompatible distance layers: tropical water under a glacial horizon, limestone houses beneath a ringed dawn, or pine-covered skerries facing desert mesas. Preserve a coherent local light source so the scene feels blended rather than randomly collaged.
Background profile: Warm-Neutral; Moist; archipelago; adventurous, wistful, socially connected; variable beach and rock friction.
DESERTS, SALT, AND DRYLANDS
34. The Red Glass Erg
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: The Sahara, Namib dunes, Atacama salt deserts, Wadi Rum, and red Australian deserts.

Landscape: Red dunes contain translucent glass layers formed when an ancient environmental proof executed through the sand. Wind exposes geometric cross-sections that can be read as both geology and unfinished mathematics.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — A Crafted World uses dune movement to perform long-duration proofs without freezing the desert’s ecology. Era One — Scholars overvalue predictable proof results and neglect the organisms that disturb them. Era Two — The proof system is simplified, leaving only several keystone equations and the water-finding behavior of local life. Era Three — Nomadic Paths use glass strata as seasonal maps. A common myth says the desert thinks in angles; the source does not confirm that the landscape is a person.
Present condition: Stable at large scale, with rare proof-storms that redraw travel routes.
Corruption: 2 — Logical function survives but its interpretation has drifted.

Aesthetic brief: Deep red-orange dunes, black rock fins, and clear glass seams glowing at low sun. Wind uncovers diagram-like shapes without using modern interface icons. During a proof-storm, sand moves in straight sheets and casts shadows before the dunes arrive.
Background profile: Hot; Bonedry; dune/proof biome; severe, luminous, meditative; low sand friction. Bonedry conditions may align with reduced parasite risk but greater fatigue or hunger pressure.
Why the glass is surreal

The glass strata are physical residues of an Era Zero environmental proof performed through moving sand. They are both geology and computation: the dunes remain a desert ecosystem while their long-term movement also carries a deterministic intellectual structure.

Era One scholars increasingly valued the predictable proof and neglected the organisms whose tracks, burrows, and migrations interrupted it. Era Three nomadic Paths instead read the exposed strata as seasonal maps, allowing the surviving function to acquire a different use.

Proof-storms reveal the remaining mismatch between desert process and ancient logic. Sand can advance in straight sheets or cast a shadow before the dune arrives, but the source does not establish that the desert is conscious.

35. The Salt Mirror Archive
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: Salar de Uyuni, Makgadikgadi Pans, Bonneville Salt Flats, and shallow seasonal lakes.
Landscape: A vast salt flat becomes a perfect sky mirror after rain. Beneath the crust lies a compressed archive that can only display records by reflecting them into the sky.

36. The Marble Dune Cemetery
Status: Proposed.
Real-world basis: Egypt’s White Desert, Lençóis Maranhenses, ancient necropolises, and eroded marble quarries.

Landscape: Pale dunes flow through rows of abstract stone forms. They are not graves in a human sense. Each marker denotes a world-law, body affordance, or ecological relation intentionally allowed to end during the Great Reduction.

Mini timeline: Era Two — Reduction councils create markers so eliminated possibilities will not be mistaken for failures never considered. The site records decisions without keeping every lost system active. Era Three — Wind exposes and covers different markers. Local peoples call it a cemetery because the old distinction between ended law, ended person, and ended habitat is no longer fully available. Some Num Seekers excavate the dunes hoping that a named loss can be restored.

Why the rain is surreal
In the city, rain is weather, infrastructure, public art, civic messaging, and shared music at the same time.

Era Zero runoff rhythms carried water while also making neighborhoods recognizable to one another. Era One standards made those rhythms clearer but increasingly repetitive. After the Reduction, Era Three communities renewed the system with improvised gutters, drums, leaves, tanks, and chimes, so living local music now overlaps with old official messages.

Corruption occurs when surviving controls confuse a channel’s physical destination with its former semantic destination. One district can receive another district’s color and rhythm. During a maintenance reversal, runoff can climb toward an inactive reservoir even while ordinary rain continues to fall. The water is not behaving randomly; it is obeying an older civic instruction that no longer matches the present city.

Biome design rules for future additions

Use real-world references as visual research, not as one-to-one cultural copies. Combine climate, geology, ecology, infrastructure, and social use rather than attaching decorative motifs from unrelated cultures.

Give every corruption a cause connected to Cyberpath history: archive loss, language drift, world folding, over-optimization, preservation panic, automatic restoration, body-scale translation, Dimming, or External Gate simplification.
Let high-corruption places contain ordinary life. Markets, meals, play, teaching, rest, illness, migration, and care should be visible even where geometry or history is unstable.
Let low-corruption places still contain conflict and uncertainty. Preservation does not guarantee justice, correct interpretation, or continued relevance.

Separate ecological succession from damage. Coral covering a plaza, mangroves growing through glass, or a forest reclaiming an access port can be life continuing rather than a failure to restore the old form.
When blending biomes, define the surviving keystone relationship that makes the blend viable. Avoid mixtures that exist only for spectacle.

For game backgrounds, keep a readable foreground surface, a horizon or depth cue, one primary motion motif, and one corruption clue. Additional history can live in alternate states, weather variants, ruins, and interactable details.
REAL-WORLD, WORLD-TRADITION, AND LOCATION RELATIONSHIP GUIDE
How the original locations connect to recognizable landscapes, newer biome locations, and Cyberpath’s World traditions
Use of real-world references

These references identify geology, ecology, scale, light, architecture, movement, and lived use that artists can study. They are not literal claims that a human country, monument, or culture was copied into the Codex. A Cyberpath location may resemble a real place because the DBA inherited human archives, because similar problems produce similar forms, because World Fold Stewards joined compatible systems, or because the External Gate translates an unfamiliar structure into imagery a player can understand.
World-tradition key
Continuity Worlds are reflected by strata, fossils, tree rings, glaciers, cairns, archives, ancestral roads, and places whose meaning depends on what remains through change.
Wild Worlds are reflected by reefs, wetlands, migrating islands, fire ecologies, forests, grasslands, predator-prey systems, succession, and landscapes that cannot be reduced to a finished design.
Crafted Worlds are reflected by terraces, gardens, resonant canyons, stepwells, engineered weather, civic water systems, responsive architecture, and physical law used as collaborative art.
Pilgrim Worlds are reflected by passes, roads, islands, waystations, body-change environments, underways, and distances that transform the traveler rather than merely transport them.
Quiet Worlds are reflected by fog forests, caves, slow archives, restricted observation, deep ice, sheltered ecologies, and places that resist constant access.
Open Worlds are reflected by ports, markets, shared cities, crossroads, translation halls, civic reservoirs, and places maintained through exchange among unlike inhabitants.
These are traditions rather than exclusive nations. A place can belong to several at once, change its emphasis across eras, or preserve only a fragment of an older tradition.

1. Cacheboard, the Unintended Board

Real-world analogue: An archaeological tell, a wall covered by generations of public notices, a market message board, and a reused archive basement. New writing sits over old writing, while discarded labels and damaged paper preserve conversations no official institution meant to keep.
World relation: Early precursor to Continuity and Open World practice. It preserves accidental witness while allowing exchange among systems that do not yet possess a formal public space.

2. The Layered Cache

Real-world analogue: Fossil-bearing desert badlands and exposed geological strata—places such as Dinosaur Provincial Park in Alberta, the Hell Creek badlands, the Painted Desert, and North African fossil beds. Wind and erosion reveal different ages as visible bands. A fossil can be found because a layer is exposed, but exposure also begins its destruction.

Visual translation: The Outer Cache resembles loose scree, wind-cut surface stone, and recently deposited sand where decoys and routing signs are easily replaced. The Working Cache resembles an active dig face with scaffolds, paths, tools, and newly exposed material. The Memory Cache resembles fossil-bearing beds in which continuity marks lie in relationship to the layer around them. The Deep Cache resembles buried strata, compressed bone beds, petroleum-dark shale, or a sealed canyon wall whose contents cannot be exposed without changing them.

World relation: Primarily Continuity and Quiet World logic. Continuity depends on the order and relationship of layers; Quiet practice limits excavation because preservation is not the same as permanent public access.

Connection to newer locations: It directly relates to the Marble Dune Cemetery, Salt Mirror Archive, Glacial Memory Fjord, Redwood Rain Vault, and River of Deferred Reflections. Each is another method of storing history in landscape rather than in a conventional library.

Abstract or metaphorical relation: Memory is stratigraphy, not a pile of interchangeable files. Context is part of the record. Digging deeper can reveal truth, but it can also destroy protection, mix eras, remove provenance, or awaken material a community was not prepared to interpret.

Status: Proposed; independent of the story archive.
Type: Hidden room inside an apparently outdoor background.
Real-world basis: Stage cycloramas, panoramic murals, desert mirages, observation decks, and painted theatrical horizons.
World relation: Crafted and Quiet World traditions.

Discovery: The distant horizon shifts slightly when the same visitor rests in the foreground on several separate visits. Walking toward the horizon never works. The room opens only when the visitor turns away and listens for movement behind the painted distance.

Mini timeline: Era Zero — The chamber teaches perspective and the limits of visual certainty. Era One — It becomes a fashionable illusion room and loses its educational context. Era Two — The outer teaching facility is reduced, while the horizon mechanism remains because it doubles as insulation. Era Three — A Nest grows in front of it without knowing a room exists behind the sky.
Present condition: Structurally intact, rarely entered, and filled with obsolete perspective controls.
Corruption: 1 — Preserved mechanism with lost purpose.

Aesthetic brief: A normal meadow, desert, or coast whose horizon is almost too perfect. Behind it lies a narrow catwalk full of painted suns, cloud shutters, depth screens, and maintenance ladders. The secret room should feel handmade rather than sinister.
Metaphorical function: What appears infinitely far away may be a surface maintained nearby. Perspective is useful without being the whole truth.
Why the horizon is surreal

The room makes distance behave like a nearby maintained object. A meadow, desert, or coast appears to continue into an ordinary horizon, yet the apparent far distance is a painted surface with cloud shutters, depth screens, stored suns, ladders, and a narrow service catwalk immediately behind it. The chamber’s preserved mechanism turns perspective into architecture.

Its access rule deepens that effect. Walking toward the horizon never reaches it; the room opens only after repeated rests, when the visitor turns away and listens for movement behind the painted distance. The mechanism survives, but the teaching context that once explained the limits of visual certainty has been lost.

VOLUME III DESIGN RULES
These locations are independent concepts. A designer may place them near established regions, but no placement should imply an unrecorded story event or the intact survival of an ancient DBA person.
Hidden rooms should contain a continuing function, ecology, community, ethical problem, or ordinary use. They should not exist only to hold treasure or lore exposition.

Discovery conditions should reveal something about the place: patience for a Quiet room, cooperative balance for shared transit, care for a domestic refuge, seasonal observation for an ecology, or refusal of ownership for common ground.
Pocket biomes need complete survival relationships at their own scale—energy, food, waste, shelter, reproduction, maintenance, succession, or a clearly acknowledged dependency on a larger world.

Corruption should remain specific. A room may have lost labels, merged seasons, reversed orientation, confused restoration records, broken access, or inconsistent scale. Avoid interchangeable visual static.

The game interface may simplify any of these spaces into a readable background, dungeon room, care area, travel node, or minigame scene, but the underlying location remains larger than its screen representation.

Language descent
At the Root, a place has a stable game-facing noun: beach, city, room, forest, gate, or archive.
One layer down, Era Three communities supply local names based on food, danger, body scale, ritual, and remembered use.

Below that, Path dialects and Old Sound fragments describe relationships rather than fixed objects: a door becomes an allowed crossing; a road becomes a sequence of recognized replies; weather becomes a system changing without damage.
Deeper still, reduced Codex language describes function: shelter, translate, witness, feed, heal, conceal, synchronize, or maintain.

In the deepest surviving Full Speech structures, language can also be proof, permission, mathematics, environmental action, and world law. The place changes because the expression is part of the process that maintains it.

At protocol depth, the apparent “location” may resolve into anchors, witness chains, access relationships, continuity marks, maintenance dependencies, and unresolved states. A room can become a relation that several systems agree to keep possible.
No invented ancient vocabulary is required for this map. The descent describes semantic behavior while leaving the complete language canon intact.

Hidden-folder behavior in the game interface
The first world map should expose Root, Gateway, Settled World, Living Biomes, Routes, Memory, and Folded regions as broad categories without revealing every child.

Dotfolders become visible through play and relationship rather than completion percentage alone. A hidden kitchen appears through care; a Quiet biome through patience; a body-keyed route through embodiment; a civic neutral zone through refusal of ownership.

Deeper folders may display more corrupted labels. Letters can become chord fragments, directional marks, overlapping local names, or function descriptions, but the interface should preserve an accessible player-readable label alongside them.
When a place is discovered, the map should record the player’s route and the cyber-pet’s recognition of the place. It should not imply that the save file contains the entire place or person.
Some folders may remain hidden permanently in one playthrough because the relevant relationship, body form, season, or ethical choice never occurs. Their absence is not failure.
Corruption presentation by depth
At shallow depth, corruption appears as weathering, repairs, local renaming, or one missing route.
At middle depth, several eras occupy the same space, seasons disagree, maps alter paths, and architectural scale no longer matches present bodies.
At language-active depth, labels become actions. Speaking, sounding, naming, promising, refusing, or witnessing can open and close spatial possibilities.
At deep semantic depth, nouns stop being reliable. “Door,” “room,” “river,” “person,” and “archive” may describe one maintained relationship from different viewpoints.
At unresolved depth, the map should state uncertainty rather than force a single answer. It may preserve multiple names, conflicting paths, or a question mark folder.
